ig_caption:
Depth First Search (DFS) Traversal on Real Street Maps — What happens when DFS explores city intersections ⚡

We turn Amsterdam (Centrum) streets into a graph: intersections = nodes, streets = edges. Then DFS starts at a chosen node and keeps going down the current branch as far as it can—using a stack (iterative) or recursion (recursive)—before it backtracks.

In the visualization, notice:
• The “frontier” is LIFO: the most recently discovered neighbor gets explored next.
• The traversal order depends on neighbor sorting (change it → different route).
• DFS finds *a* path (or visit order), not the shortest path—BFS is the usual shortest-path choice.

Takeaway: DFS is great for exploring structure, detecting components, and doing classic graph-theory tasks—just don’t assume “deep” means “short.”

Debate question: Would DFS feel faster here than BFS in a dense street grid—yes or no?
